idiom_name: jscodeshift find/filter/replaceWith collections over ast-types paths, recast for printing
implementation_notes: jscodeshift wraps recast and ast-types: api.jscodeshift(source).find(j.CallExpression) returns a collection of paths, filter narrows it with a predicate over node fields, and replaceWith, insertBefore or remove apply the action while recast reprints only the changed regions, so formatting survives. The traversal is the collection API's, the pattern is a node type plus a predicate (or a shallow object filter, which does not deep-match), and the action is the replacement call - the closest JavaScript gets to a rule table without a query language. Babel's @babel/traverse is the compiler-plugin counterpart (visitor keys plus replaceWith and replaceWithMultiple); choose jscodeshift when the job is a batch codemod over files.
pitfalls: find(j.X, { field: value }) compares properties shallowly, so a structural condition must be written as a predicate; an object filter that expects deep matching silently matches too much or nothing.
Replacing a node rebuilds its ancestors: comments, parentheses and ASI-relevant tokens are not carried over automatically, and recast then reprints the node without them.
TypeScript input needs the matching parser (parser: 'ts' or 'tsx'), and Babel and TypeScript node shapes differ in places, so a pattern copied between toolchains can match nothing.

variants.name: ESLint selectors (esquery) as declarative subtree patterns
variants.idiom_name: esquery selector strings (node types, attributes, combinators, :matches, :has)
variants.implementation_notes: ESLint's selector syntax is esquery, a CSS-like query language over the ESTree AST: node types, attribute existence and values, regex attributes, combinators (> child, descendant, + adjacent sibling, ~ following sibling), :not, :is/:matches, :has and :first-child/:last-child. A rule registers a listener under the selector string and receives exactly the matching nodes (:exit runs on the way out), the same strings work in configuration through no-restricted-syntax, and the fixer is the action. It is the purest declarative form in JavaScript and the reason a custom matcher is usually unnecessary - but it matches only, so the action is an ESLint fix or report rather than an arbitrary tree rewrite.
pitfalls: Attribute selectors match node properties literally: nested properties need the [attr.level2="foo"] form, and comparing the raw source form against the parsed value matches nothing.
All listeners run during one traversal, so overlapping fixes conflict and ESLint reports them instead of applying; a fix that changes the tree another listener depends on is order-dependent.
Regular expressions containing a slash are a documented esquery bug (/some\/path/ is a syntax error) and the workaround is the unicode escape.
